newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe faces budget challenge to satisfy donors.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe faces budget challenge to satisfy donors.

text.p: Zimbabwe unveils a crucial budget next week which foreign donors will study before deciding on support for a new round of economic reforms.
The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have said they are waiting for Robert Mugabe's government to rein in runaway spending and the galloping budget deficit.
The two bodies backed Zimbabwe's first phase of reforms which ended in 1995 and want to see action before they agree to support another lap.
Key Western donors suspended balance of payments support in 1995 because of the government's persistent failure to meet deficit reduction targets in the first five-year plan.

Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa said this month the deficit for the financial year ended June 30 was expected to come in at 10.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- wide of the 8.5 percent target he set himself.
The World Bank's representative to Zimbabwe, David Cook, said talks would begin after the budget had been presented.
"Once the budget comes then we will meet to discuss (aid)," he told Reuters.

IMF representative Robert Franco said the fund had worked with the government on the budget and that a new aid programme would be discussed in September. That programme would include key economic targets the Harare government would have to meet.
"We will have benchmarks every six months to assess certain indicators," he said, adding that these would include inflation, the deficit and domestic borrowing.

Zimababwe's annual inflation edged up to 21.4 percent in June from May's 20.7 percent and local economic analysts expect it to rise to 24 percent in the second half of the year, fuelled by high money supply growth and expected hikes in excise duties.
The budget will cover the period from July 1997 to December 1998 as the government moves to a calendar year.

"This budget is of great significance in that we really need to see a clear political commitment and will to reduce the budget deficit to reasonable levels to establish a stable macroeconomic environment to promote higher economic growth," said Danny Dube, chief economist at the Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe.

The government, anxious to avert more wildcat strikes like those which rocked the public service last year, recently awarded its workers a 30 percent pay increase effective from July 1, the beginning of the new financial year.
The wage settlements are expected to cost it an extra Z$9.1 billion (U.S. $800 million) in the new budget. ($1=Z$11.37)

Anthony Hawkins, of the University of Zimbabwe, said the government would have to raise taxes and cut spending in an effort to satisfy the demands of the bloated civil service as well as cut the deficit.
"The government has a pretty nasty amount to pick up from recent wage increases and they also need to knock off at least Z$5 billion (US$879 million)," he said.
